title: JSON Web Algorithms (JWA)
summary: This specification registers cryptographic algorithms and identifiers for use with the JSON Web Signature, JSON Web Encryption, and JSON Web Key specifications. It also defines several IANA registries for these identifiers.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the menu of secret-code methods that the JSON signing and locking formats can use, each with a name.

subtitle: The menu of named signature, key-wrapping, content-encryption and key-type algorithms that JSON Web Signature, Encryption and Key can use.

tldr.problem: The JSON-based signing, encryption and key formats (JWS, JWE, JWK) need agreed short names for the cryptographic algorithms they use, and those names should not be locked inside the format specifications themselves.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7518 defines the algorithm identifiers used in the "alg", "enc" and "kty" values, explains exactly how each algorithm is applied, sets key-size and parameter rules, and creates IANA registries so new identifiers can be added.
tldr.outcome: Implementations get a fixed vocabulary such as HS256, RS256, ES256, A128KW and A128GCM with a stated requirement level for each. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 9864.

today: RFC 7518 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 9864, so read the two together. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why the Algorithms Live in Their Own RFC
sections.content:
RFC 7518 registers cryptographic algorithms and identifiers for the JSON Web Signature (JWS), JSON Web Encryption (JWE) and JSON Web Key (JWK) specifications, all of which use JSON data structures. It also describes the semantics and operations that are specific to each algorithm and key type, and it defines several IANA registries for the identifiers.

The identifiers are kept here, rather than in the JWS, JWE and JWK documents, so those documents can stay unchanged while the set of Required, Recommended, Optional and Deprecated algorithms changes over time. Names are deliberately short because a core goal is compact representations.

The RFC also defines one helper term, Base64urlUInt: a non-negative integer written as the base64url encoding of its unsigned big-endian octets, using the minimum number of octets. Zero is written as AA.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipes for secret codes are written in a separate cookbook. That way the cookbook can get new recipes without anybody rewriting the signing and locking rules.

sections.title: Signature and MAC Algorithms for JWS
sections.content:
Section 3 lists the alg values for JWS. HS256, HS384 and HS512 are HMACs with SHA-2. The key MUST be at least as large as the hash output, for example 256 bits for HS256. The RS family (RS256, RS384, RS512) uses RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 and the PS family uses RSASSA-PSS with MGF1; both require an RSA key of 2048 bits or larger. The ES family uses ECDSA with the P-256, P-384 and P-521 curves.

For ECDSA the signature is the two numbers R and S, each written as a fixed-length big-endian octet sequence and joined as R then S. Leading zero octets MUST NOT be dropped. That gives 64 octets for ES256, 96 for ES384 and 132 for ES512, and a verifier must fail the check if the length is wrong. A comparison of an HMAC against the received signature MUST be done in constant time to thwart timing attacks.

Finally, none defines an Unsecured JWS: it has no integrity protection and its signature is the empty octet sequence. Implementations MUST NOT accept it by default, and applications MUST NOT signal acceptance of it at a global level; they SHOULD signal acceptance per object.

The requirement column uses "+" to mean the requirement is likely to be raised in a future version, so ES256 is marked Recommended+ while HS256 is the only Required signature or MAC algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature is like a wax seal on a letter. The menu names a few kinds of seals, and the rule for the blank "no seal" option is: never trust a letter with no seal unless you were told to expect one.

sections.title: Key Management Algorithms for JWE
sections.content:
A JWE encrypts the message with a Content Encryption Key (CEK). Section 4 defines how that CEK reaches the recipient, using the alg header. The options are:

  • Key encryption with RSA: RSA1_5 (RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5), RSA-OAEP (OAEP with default parameters, which are SHA-1 and MGF1 with SHA-1) and RSA-OAEP-256 (SHA-256). Keys of 2048 bits or larger MUST be used.
  • AES Key Wrap: A128KW, A192KW, A256KW.
  • Direct use of a shared symmetric key as the CEK: dir, with an empty JWE Encrypted Key.
  • ECDH-ES key agreement, either direct (ECDH-ES) or with the CEK wrapped (ECDH-ES+A128KW and the 192 and 256 variants).
  • AES GCM key wrapping: A128GCMKW, A192GCMKW, A256GCMKW.
  • Password-based: PBES2-HS256+A128KW, PBES2-HS384+A192KW, PBES2-HS512+A256KW.

ECDH-ES uses a fresh ephemeral public key for every key agreement, sent in the epk header, and derives the key with the Concat KDF using SHA-256. Optional apu and apv headers carry information about the producer and the recipient. AES GCM key wrapping requires a 96-bit IV (header iv) and a 128-bit tag (header tag).

For PBES2 the salt input in p2s MUST be at least 8 octets and freshly random for every encryption. The iteration count goes in p2c, and a minimum of 1000 is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is locked with a key, and that key has to get to the other person safely. The menu lists ways to do that: put it in a locked box, agree on it in secret, or make it from a password.

sections.title: Content Encryption Algorithms
sections.content:
Section 5 defines the enc values, which say how the message itself is encrypted and integrity-protected. All of them use an initialization vector and produce ciphertext plus an authentication tag. There are two families.

AES_CBC_HMAC_SHA2 combines AES in CBC mode with PKCS #7 padding and an HMAC. The input key K is split: the first part is the MAC key and the final part is the encryption key (the opposite order from the algorithm name). The tag is the HMAC over the additional authenticated data, the IV, the ciphertext and the length of the additional data in bits, truncated to a set length. A 128-bit IV is generated randomly or pseudorandomly. On decryption the tag is checked first, and if it does not match the operation fails.

AES GCM (A128GCM, A192GCM, A256GCM) requires a 96-bit IV and a 128-bit authentication tag regardless of key size.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the part that locks the actual letter. It scrambles the letter and also adds a tamper-proof sticker, so the receiver can tell if anyone changed it on the way.

sections.title: Key Types and Parameters for JWK
sections.content:
Section 6 defines three key types for the JWK kty member: EC (elliptic curve), RSA and oct (an octet sequence, used for symmetric keys). RSA and oct are Required, and EC is Recommended+.

An EC public key uses crv (one of P-256, P-384, P-521), x and y. Each coordinate must be the full size for the curve, for example 66 octets for P-521, and point compression is not supported. A private key adds d. An RSA public key uses n (modulus) and e (exponent) as Base64urlUInt values; the exponent 65537 is the octets 1, 0, 1 and encodes as AQAB. RSA private keys add d and, as optimizations, p, q, dp, dq and qi; oth appears only when more than two primes were used. A symmetric key is stored in k.
sections.plainLanguage: A key can be written down as a little form with labelled boxes. Different kinds of keys have different boxes to fill in, and this section lists them.

sections.title: The IANA Registries
sections.content:
The RFC creates registries so new identifiers can be added without a new RFC for each: the JSON Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms registry, Header Parameter names, the JWE Compression Algorithms registry (initial entry DEF, DEFLATE), JSON Web Key Types, JSON Web Key Parameters and JSON Web Key Elliptic Curve.

New values need Specification Required after a three-week review on a mailing list, on the advice of one or more Designated Experts. The experts check whether a request duplicates existing functionality, whether it is generally applicable and whether the description is clear. Algorithms being registered should be currently credible or be registered as Deprecated or Prohibited.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a public sign-up book for new code names. A few helpers check that a new name is useful and not a copy before it goes in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC stresses cryptographic agility: algorithms weaken over time, so implementations should be modular and ready to change the algorithms they support. Specific cautions include:

  • RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5: RFC 3447 asks people not to adopt it for new applications, but it is included for interoperability because it is commonly implemented.
  • AES GCM: a key MUST NOT be used more than 2^32 times, and an IV MUST NOT ever be reused with the same key.
  • Unsecured JWS: accepting none globally lets an attacker send an unsigned object over a channel that should require a signature.
  • Denial of service: implementations should set upper limits on accepted key sizes.
  • Passwords: PBES2 is only as strong as the password and the iteration count; a password of 16 to 128 octets is RECOMMENDED for PBES2-HS256+A128KW.
  • Key reuse: it is NOT RECOMMENDED to reuse the whole set of key material when encrypting keys.

Several other topics, such as timing attacks and matching algorithm strengths, are delegated to sections of the JWS, JWE and JWK specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say: do not reuse a one-time lock number, do not accept unsealed letters by default, use strong passwords, and be ready to switch to better codes when old ones get weak.
